title: Oboe
wiki_lead:
The oboe ( OH-boh) is a type of double-reed woodwind instrument. Oboes are usually made of wood, but may also be made of synthetic materials, such as plastic, resin, or hybrid composites.
The most common type of oboe, the soprano oboe pitched in C, measures roughly 65 cm (25+1⁄2 in) long and has metal keys, a conical bore and a flared bell. Sound is produced by blowing into the reed at a sufficient air pressure, causing it to vibrate with the air column. The distinctive tone is versatile and has been described as "bright". When the word oboe is used alone, it is generally taken to mean the soprano member rather than other instruments of the family, such as the bass oboe, the cor anglais (English horn), or oboe d'amore.
Today, the oboe is commonly used as orchestral or solo instrument in symphony orchestras, concert bands and chamber ensembles. The oboe is especially used in classical music, film music, some genres of folk music, and is occasionally heard in jazz, rock, pop, and popular music. The oboe is widely recognized as the instrument that tunes the orchestra with its distinctive A.
A musician who plays the oboe is called an oboist.

Sound
In comparison to other modern woodwind instruments, the soprano oboe is sometimes referred to as having a "bright and penetrating" voice. The Sprightly Companion, an instruction book published by Henry Playford in 1695, describes the oboe as "Majestical and Stately, and not much Inferior to the Trumpet". In the play Angels in America the sound is described as like "that of a duck if the duck were a songbird". The rich timbre is derived from its conical bore (as opposed to the generally cylindrical bore of flutes and   clarinets). As a result, oboes are easier to hear over other instruments in large ensembles due to their penetrating sound. The highest note is a semitone lower than the nominally highest note of the B♭ clarinet. Since the clarinet has a wider range, the lowest note of the B♭ clarinet is significantly deeper (a minor sixth) than the lowest note of the oboe.
Music for the standard oboe is written in concert pitch (i.e., it is not a transposing instrument), and the instrument has a soprano range, usually from B♭3 to G6. Orchestras tune to a concert A played by the first oboe. According to the League of American Orchestras, this is done because the pitch is secure and its penetrating sound makes it ideal for tuning. Additionally, the oboe is the tuning instrument of choice because it is the one instrument in the orchestra that cannot move part of the instrument to change the pitch. Clarinets and flutes can lengthen their instruments, brass can adjust their tuning slides, and strings can turn their tuning pegs. To adjust pitch on an oboe to the same degree, the oboist must make adjustments to their reed. Because of the lack of flexibility in instrument adjustment, all other instruments change theirs slightly to match. 
The pitch of the oboe is affected by the way in which the reed is made. The reed has a significant effect on the sound. Variations in cane and other construction materials, the age of the reed, and differences in scrape and length all affect the pitch. German and French reeds, for instance, differ in many ways, causing the sound to vary accordingly. Weather conditions such as temperature and humidity also affect the pitch. Skilled oboists adjust their embouchure to compensate for these factors. Subtle manipulation of embouchure and air pressure allows the oboist to express timbre and dynamics.


Reeds

The oboe uses a double reed, similar to that used for the bassoon. Most professional oboists make their reeds to suit their individual needs. By making their reeds, oboists can precisely control factors such as tone color, intonation, and responsiveness. They can also account for individual embouchure, oral cavity, oboe angle, and air support.

grok_lead: The oboe is a double-reed woodwind instrument classified as a conical-bore aerophone, distinguished by its piercing, reedy timbre that blends lyricism with technical precision. Typically constructed from dense hardwoods like grenadilla or African blackwood for professional models, with student versions often using durable resin or plastic, the oboe features a narrow internal bore that flares slightly toward a flared bell, enabling its characteristic sound projection. It comprises three primary sectionsâthe upper joint, lower joint, and bellâconnected via tenon-and-socket joints, with a complex keywork system of up to 45 silver-plated keys, rods, and springs that covers 21 tone holes for fully chromatic playability. The sound is produced by vibrating a double reed made from Arundo donax cane, folded and tied to a metal staple inserted into the top joint, requiring precise embouchure control from the player. Originating from ancient double-reed precursors traceable to around 2800 B.C. in ancient Egypt and evolving through medieval European forms such as the shawm, the oboe emerged in its recognizable Baroque configuration in France during the mid-17th century. By 1657, it had debuted in French orchestral settings, with key innovations like the addition of keys for better intonation and the standardization of its three-joint design occurring through the 18th century, solidifying its role by 1750 as an essential melodic voice in symphony orchestras. The modern conservatory system, influenced by 19th-century French makers like Triebert and drawing from the Boehm flute mechanism, expanded its range from roughly Bâ­ 3 to A 6 âspanning nearly three octavesâand enhanced fingerings for greater agility. In contemporary music, the oboe serves as a cornerstone of orchestral, chamber, and solo repertoires, prized for its ability to convey pastoral tenderness or haunting expressiveness, as heard in works from Bach concertos to 20th-century pieces by composers like Britten. The principal oboist traditionally sounds the concert A (440 Hz) to tune ensembles, underscoring its tuning reference status. Playing demands advanced breath control, reed adjustment, and hand positioningâoften starting at age 10â11 under private instructionâwhile variants like the English horn ( cor anglais), oboe d'amore, and bass oboe extend the family's tonal palette across lower registers.
